As a brief intermezzo, let's take a look at **VS Code**,
the text editor you'll use throughout the course to write code and documentation.

## What is VS Code?

VS Code is basically a **fancy text editor**.
Its full name is Visual Studio Code, while the version you can use in your browser
at OSC is called "Code Server".

To emphasize the additional functionality relative to basic text editors like Notepad and TextEdit,
editors like VS Code are also referred to as **IDEs**: *Integrated Development Environments*.
The RStudio program is another good example of an IDE.
Just like RStudio is an IDE for R, VS Code will be our IDE for shell code^[
Some advantages of VS Code: Works with all operating systems, is free, and open source;
it has an integrated terminal with a Unix shell; it is available at OSC OnDemand;
it is very popular and heavily developed].

## Starting VS Code at OSC

- Log in to OSC's OnDemand portal at <https://ondemand.osc.edu>.

- In the blue top bar, select `Interactive Apps` and near the bottom of the
  dropdown menu, click `Code Server`.

- Interactive Apps like VS Code **run on compute nodes** (not login nodes).
  Because compute nodes always need to be "reserved",
  we have to fill out a form and specify the following details:
  - The **Cluster** that we want to use: `pitzer`
  - The **Account**, i.e., the OSC Project to be billed for the compute node usage: `PAS3493`
  - The **Number of hours** we want to make a reservation for: `2`
  - This time, leave the **Working Directory** (starting point) for the program blank
  - The **App Code Server version**: `4.8.3` (this should be the only available option)

  _TODO - Add screenshot_

- Click `Launch` and you'll be sent to the _My Interactive Sessions_ page
  with a card for your job at the top.

- First, your job may be *Queued* for some seconds
  (i.e., waiting for computing resources to be assigned to it),
  but it should soon switch to *Starting* and then
  be ready for usage (*Running*) in another couple of seconds:

![](../img/ondemand_vscode_running2.png){fig-align="center" width="75%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the OSC OnDemand page shown when the Code Server job has started running." .lightbox}

- Once the blue **Connect to VS Code** button appears,
  click that to open VS Code in a new browser tab.

- When VS Code opens, you may get a pop-up similar to this — check the box and click “Yes”:

![](../img/vscode-trust2.png){fig-align="center" width="50%" fig-alt="A screenshot of a popup you may get when first opening a folder in VS Code." .lightbox}

- You'll also see a Welcome document ---
  you don't have to go through any steps that may be suggested there.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
_Congratulations: you have started your first compute job at OSC!_ &nbsp; [🥳]{style="font-size: 1.2em;"}
:::

### Side bars

By default, the (wide) **Side Bar** will show a file explorer,
where you can see files, create new folders and files, and so on.

_TODO ADD SCREENSHOT_

The **Activity Bar** (narrow side bar) on the far left has:

- A {{< fa bars >}} ("hamburger menu"), with menu items like `File`
  (those you often find in a program's top bar)

- Icons to toggle between options for the wide Side Bar:
  we'll talk about those in a later session

- A {{< fa cog >}} (cog wheel icon) in the bottom, with access to:
  
  - Settings, where you can configure VS Code
  - "Command Palette", a search bar to find and run all VS Code functionality
  
### A folder as a starting point

VS Code takes a specific
**folder as a starting point in all parts of the program**:

- In its file explorer
- When saving files
- In the Unix shell its terminal

{{< fa user-edit >}} Click `File` > `Open Folder` and then enter your
personal folder in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people`
(for example, I will select `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer`).
_This will cause the program to reload._

### Terminal (with a Unix shell)

{{< fa user-edit >}} **Open a terminal** by clicking
{{< fa bars >}}   > `Terminal` > `New Terminal`.
We'll start using this terminal in the next lecture.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Your Turn

1. In the cog wheel {{< fa cog >}} menu, click `Themes` > `Color Theme`
   to explore VS Code color themes and optionally **change the color theme** to your liking.

2. You can **resize panes** by hovering your cursor over the borders between them and then dragging.
   Try doing this with the border between the Primary Side Bar and the editor pane,
   and that between the panel with the terminal and the editor pane.

### Editor pane and `Welcome` document

The main part of the VS Code is the **editor pane**.
Here, you can open scripts and other types of text files, images, and so on.
Like in a web browser and other modern editors, you can have multiple tabs open.

Whenever you open VS Code,
an editor tab with a `Welcome` document is automatically opened.
This provides some help and shortcuts to recently opened files and folders.

{{< fa user-edit >}} **Create and save a new file:**

1. Open a new file in the editor pane:
   Click the hamburger menu <i class="fa fa-bars"></i> > `File` > `New File`.
2. Save the file (<kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>S</kbd>) within your `week02` dir
   as a Markdown file, e.g. `markdown-intro.md`.
